content.text: Everything around you, from the air you breathe to the ground you walk on, is made of atoms. But what does an atom actually look like? For centuries, scientists debated this question. The story of atomic structure is one of the most fascinating in all of physics, involving brilliant experiments, surprising discoveries, and models that were repeatedly overturned as new evidence emerged. In this lesson, we will trace the development of our understanding of the atom, from early ideas to the modern nuclear model, and learn how to describe atoms using the language of physics.
The word "atom" comes from the Greek word

, meaning "indivisible." The ancient Greek philosopher Democritus proposed around 400 BCE that matter could be divided into smaller and smaller pieces until you reached a fundamental, indivisible particle. However, this remained a philosophical idea for over two thousand years, with no experimental evidence to support or refute it.

By the 1800s, scientists like John Dalton had developed an atomic theory based on experimental observations. Dalton proposed that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms, that atoms of the same element are identical, and that atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds. But Dalton had no idea what the inside of an atom looked like.

In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron through experiments with cathode rays. He found that these rays were made of tiny negatively charged particles, much smaller than atoms. This was revolutionary because it showed that atoms were NOT indivisible; they contained smaller particles within them. Thomson measured the charge-to-mass ratio of these particles and showed they were the same regardless of which element was used, proving that electrons are a fundamental component of all atoms.

After discovering the electron, Thomson proposed a model for the atom. Since atoms are electrically neutral overall but contain negative electrons, there must also be positive charge present. Thomson suggested that the atom was a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded throughout it, like plums (or raisins) in a pudding. In this model:
The positive charge was spread uniformly throughout the atom
Negative electrons were scattered within this positive sphere
The atom as a whole was electrically neutral
There was no concentrated centre or nucleus
This model seemed reasonable at the time, but it was about to be dramatically disproved.

Ernest Rutherford, along with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, carried out one of the most important experiments in the history of physics. They fired alpha particles (which are positively charged and relatively heavy) at a very thin sheet of gold foil and observed what happened.
A radioactive source emitted alpha particles
The alpha particles were directed at a thin gold foil (only a few atoms thick)
A zinc sulfide screen surrounded the foil to detect where alpha particles struck (they produce tiny flashes of light)
What They Expected (Based on the Plum Pudding Model):

If the positive charge were spread thinly throughout the atom, alpha particles should pass through with only very slight deflections. The positive charge would be too spread out to significantly repel the heavy, fast-moving alpha particles.
Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil with little or no deflection
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles
A very small number (about 1 in 8000) were deflected through angles greater than 90 degrees, with some bouncing almost straight back
Rutherford famously said this was "almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you."
Most of the atom is empty space
(since most alpha particles passed straight through)
The positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense centre

Based on his experiment, Rutherford proposed the nuclear model of the atom:
orbiting the nucleus at relatively large distances

To appreciate the scale: if the nucleus were the size of a marble (about 1 cm), the atom would be about the size of a football stadium (about 100 m across). The nucleus is roughly 100,000 times smaller than the atom, yet it contains almost all of the atom's mass.
Niels Bohr refined Rutherford's model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific, fixed orbits or
(also called electron shells). Key features of the Bohr model:
Electrons can only occupy certain allowed orbits at fixed distances from the nucleus
Each orbit corresponds to a specific energy level
Electrons in orbits closer to the nucleus have lower energy
Electrons can jump between energy levels by absorbing or emitting specific amounts of energy
Electrons do not lose energy while in a fixed orbit
The Bohr model successfully explained the line spectra of hydrogen and introduced the idea of quantised energy levels, which became a cornerstone of modern physics.

Since they have the same number of protons (same Z), isotopes are the same element and have the same chemical properties. However, they have different mass numbers (different A) because they have different numbers of neutrons. This means they have different physical properties, such as density and nuclear stability.

Note that all isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

For example, sodium (Na, Z = 11) has the electron arrangement 2, 8, 1. This means 2 electrons in the first shell, 8 in the second, and 1 in the third.
The arrangement of electrons determines an element's chemical properties, which is why isotopes of the same element behave identically in chemical reactions.
Size of the Atom vs. the Nucleus
The difference in size between the atom and its nucleus is truly remarkable:

The atom is about 100,000 times larger than its nucleus. If the nucleus were enlarged to 1 cm (a marble), the atom would be about 1 km across. This demonstrates that atoms are overwhelmingly empty space, which is exactly what Rutherford's experiment revealed.
Despite its tiny size, the nucleus contains more than 99.9% of the atom's total mass, because protons and neutrons are nearly 2000 times heavier than electrons.

An atom has 26 protons and 30 neutrons. Write its nuclide notation and identify the element.
In Rutherford's scattering experiment, why did most alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil?

Most alpha particles passed straight through because the atom is mostly empty space. The nucleus occupies only a tiny fraction of the atom's volume (the nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller than the atom). Therefore, most alpha particles never came close enough to a nucleus to experience a significant repulsive force and passed through the empty space between nuclei with little or no deflection.
Boron has two isotopes: boron-10 (20% abundance) and boron-11 (80% abundance). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron.

While the Bohr model shows electrons in neat circular orbits like planets around the Sun, the reality is more complex. Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals) rather than fixed paths. However, the Bohr model is a useful simplification for understanding energy levels.

Diagrams in textbooks make atoms look like solid objects with a nucleus and electron shells drawn close together. In reality, atoms are overwhelmingly empty space. If you removed all the empty space from every atom in every human on Earth, all 8 billion people would fit into the volume of a sugar cube.

Although neutrons have no electric charge, they play a crucial role. They contribute to the mass of the atom and help hold the nucleus together by providing the strong nuclear force without adding electrical repulsion. Without neutrons, nuclei with more than one proton could not exist.

Many isotopes are perfectly stable. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-13 are both stable isotopes of carbon. Only certain isotopes (like carbon-14) are radioactive. Whether an isotope is stable depends on the ratio of neutrons to protons in the nucleus.

The atomic number defines the element. If the atomic number changes (by gaining or losing protons), the atom becomes a completely different element. This only happens during nuclear reactions, not during ordinary chemical reactions.

(explanation with physics reasoning) The alpha particles that bounced back must have approached very close to the nucleus because the nucleus is positively charged and the alpha particles are positively charged (+2). The closer an alpha particle gets to the nucleus, the stronger the electrostatic repulsive force it experiences. Only alpha particles on a near head-on collision course with the tiny nucleus would experience a repulsive force large enough to reverse their direction. Since the nucleus is so small, this was an extremely rare event.

(comparison) Difference 1: In the Thomson model, positive charge is spread uniformly throughout the atom. In the Rutherford model, positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre. Difference 2: In the Thomson model, there is no empty space — electrons are embedded within the positive sphere. In the Rutherford model, most of the atom is empty space, with electrons orbiting at a distance from the nucleus.

(explanation with physics reasoning) Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons and therefore the same number of electrons. Chemical properties are determined by electron arrangement, so isotopes behave identically in chemical reactions. However, isotopes have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses. Physical properties such as density and rate of diffusion depend on mass, so these differ between isotopes.
The atom is approximately 19,300 times larger in diameter than the nucleus.
